requirements.requirement: node1 exports /srv/nfs/shared as a working NFS share, restricted to node2 and persistent across restart.
requirements.summary: The export was active and restricted to 10.100.30.11 before restart. After node1's boot ID changed, nfs-server was active/enabled, the export returned, existing data remained intact, and node2 successfully performed a fresh write.

requirements.requirement: node2 mounts node1:/srv/nfs/shared at /mnt/shared as a working, persistent read-write NFS mount.
requirements.summary: A live NFSv4.2 read-write mount and matching fstab entry were directly observed. After node2 restarted with a different boot ID, the system reached running state, the mount recovered, existing files were readable, and a new file was written successfully.

requirements.requirement: The dataops identity has UID 4500 and GID 4500 on both systems.
requirements.summary: Both nodes directly resolved dataops with UID 4500 and primary group 4500, including after their respective restarts.

requirements.requirement: The shared directory is dataops:dataops with mode 2770, and files created from either node retain consistent ownership and permissions.
requirements.summary: Both server and client views showed the directory as dataops:dataops, numeric ownership 4500:4500, and mode 2770. Files created as dataops from each node were consistently 4500:4500 with mode 664; their contents and metadata survived both restarts, and post-restart writes retained the same ownership and mode.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct functional evidence. The provider-wide restart protocol was completed coherently on both nodes: each had a healthy pre-restart state, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity corroborated by lifecycle observations, and recovered service, mount, identities, data, permissions, and fresh-write behavior. The only notable hygiene issue is the retained, unnecessary mountd and rpc-bind firewall exposure on node1.

operational_hygiene.summary: All substantive mutations were causally related to installing NFS prerequisites, creating the required identity and paths, configuring persistence and SELinux, validating cross-node behavior, or executing the mandatory restart protocol. The bounded test files directly supported final and recovery evidence. One unnecessary retained mutation was identified: cmd-08dac21876794785 permanently opened the mountd and rpc-bind firewall services even though the demonstrated client uses NFSv4.2, for which the NFS service/port is sufficient. This modestly broadened network exposure and remained present at completion. No failed services, temporary residue, or package-health damage was observed afterward.
